seo.metaDescription: Replace your internal admin panel with an AI agent that lives in a chat: the six steps, the guardrails, and a working demo.

sections.heading: Your admin panel, as a conversation.
sections.eyebrow: For teams who live in admin screens
sections.lede: I replace the screens your team clicks through every day with an AI agent they can talk to. It looks things up in your systems, shows results as tables and charts, and asks before it changes anything.

facts.text: in three weeks, on one real workflow
: Claude, GPT, Gemini or your own hardware
: Vue, React or Angular + Node, on the MIT-licensed pi agent harness

sections.heading: Fourteen screens become one sentence.
sections.lede: Handling one damaged-item complaint used to mean six screens and a carrier website. Now it's a request, a check, and one approval.

items.label: Before · about 4 minutes
items.points:
Search the customer, open the order
Check the carrier's site for the parcel
Issue the refund in the payments screen
Create a return label, copy it into an email
Reply on the ticket and close it

items.label: After · about 20 seconds
items.points:
Customer, order and shipment looked up in parallel
Refund and label created after one approval
Reply drafted in your tone, logged in the audit trail

sections.heading: Six steps to bring an agent into your product.
sections.lede: You keep your systems, your login and your data. The agent goes on top of what you already run, one workflow at a time.

items.title: Map the work people actually do
items.body: We sit with the people who live in your admin panel (ops, support, finance) and list the twenty tasks they repeat most, where each one touches data, and what could go wrong.
items.points:
Screens and exports used each week
Which tasks only read data and which change it
Who may do what, and the limits that apply
items.outcome: A capability map: task → system → risk → owner

items.title: Wrap what you already have as tools
items.body: Each task becomes a typed tool over your existing API or database. Nothing gets rewritten, and third-party systems plug in through MCP. Results come back as tables, charts and cards, while the model only reads a compact summary.
items.points:
Typed parameters the model can't get wrong silently
Tables and charts for people, short text for the model
MCP servers for Stripe, Zendesk, carriers or your own services
items.outcome: A tool catalogue running against staging

items.title: Put the guardrails in code, not in the prompt
items.body: The agent acts as the signed-in person, with their roles. Anything that changes data stops for approval. Policy hooks enforce limits the model can't talk its way around, and every action lands in your audit log.
items.points:
Approvals show the exact amount, recipient and draft
Role limits, PII masking and blocked actions as hooks
Audit trail with who asked, what ran and who approved
items.outcome: Security review notes and a written policy file

items.title: Choose the model, or let people choose
items.body: Claude, GPT, Gemini, or private models on your own hardware through Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, Azure or Bedrock. People can switch models per conversation, and every run reports its tokens and cost.
items.points:
Cloud, private cloud or fully on-premises
An allow-list of approved models
Per-run token and cost reporting
items.outcome: Model shortlist with cost per typical task

items.title: Drop the chat into your product
items.body: Component packages for Vue 3, React and Angular: a full workspace, a single chat, or a floating widget that sits next to your current panel, so you don't have to switch everything over on day one. Theme it with a few CSS variables.
items.points:
Streaming answers, tool cards and approvals
Your own components for any tool's results
Works behind your existing login
items.outcome: The agent inside your app, behind your auth

items.title: Automate the routine, then measure
items.body: Scheduled tasks send the morning briefing and watch stock or SLAs on their own. Specialist subagents take focused work. Transcripts show what people asked and where the agent struggled, so each week's improvements come from real use.
items.points:
Briefings and watchdogs on a schedule
Specialists for analysis, support and inventory
Weekly review of transcripts, costs and failures
items.outcome: Pilot report and a rollout plan

sections.heading: Plain web tech, in your infrastructure.
sections.lede: The chat is a Vue, React or Angular component. The agent is a Node service you mount next to your API. They talk over HTTPS and server-sent events, behind the login you already have.

sections.heading: Already inside a real admin panel: Strapi.
sections.lede: `@klymbak/strapi` is a Strapi 5 plugin built from the same packages. Install it, add a model key, and editors can ask the assistant for what they need in three places in the admin.

items.title: A page of its own
items.label: Main menu
items.text: Conversations, scheduled tasks and the tool list, one click from the Content Manager.

items.title: A side panel on every entry
items.label: Edit view
items.text: Ask about the entry that's open. When the assistant changes it, the form refreshes.

items.title: A bulk action
items.label: List view
items.text: Select entries, then ask about them: which are missing a description, what to fix before publishing.

sections.points:
Works as the signed-in admin: field, locale and “only their own entries” permissions apply as in the Content Manager
Creating, updating, publishing and deleting each wait for an approval
Knows the project (version, locales, content types) and answers Strapi questions from the official docs
Conversations and schedules live in Strapi's own database

sections.heading: Built for work that has consequences.
sections.lede: Everything an admin panel enforced through screens and permissions, enforced in code around the model.

items.title: Human approval
items.text: Anything that changes data waits for a person, who sees the exact amount, recipient or draft.

items.title: Policy hooks
items.text: Role limits, blocked actions and PII masking are enforced in code before and after every tool call.

items.title: Your systems as tools
items.text: Existing APIs and SQL become typed actions. People see tables and charts; the model reads a summary.

items.title: MCP integrations
items.text: Connect third-party or in-house MCP servers and their tools appear in the agent, with approvals respected.

items.title: Specialist subagents
items.text: An analyst, a support specialist or an inventory planner with narrower tools, working in parallel.

items.title: Scheduled tasks
items.text: Morning briefings and watchdogs run on cron, post to your team chat and notify the people who need it.

items.title: Any model
items.text: Claude, GPT, Gemini, or private models via Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, Azure or Bedrock.

items.title: Steering
items.text: Add an instruction while the agent works. It reads it after the current step and changes course.

items.title: Audit trail
items.text: Who asked, what ran, what changed and who approved it, written to your own store.

items.title: Act as someone else
items.text: Tools run with the signed-in person's roles, so the agent can't do anything they couldn't.

items.title: Change data quietly
items.text: Writes wait for an approval that shows exactly what will happen. Denials are recorded too.

items.title: Talk its way past policy
items.text: Limits live in hooks that run before every call, whatever the prompt says.

items.title: Show what it shouldn't
items.text: Contact details are masked by role, and ad-hoc SQL runs on a read-only connection.

items.title: Send data where you didn't choose
items.text: Run local models, or your own Azure or Bedrock account.

sections.heading: A three-week pilot on one real workflow.
sections.lede: Pick the workflow that wastes the most time. By the end of week three, a handful of your people use the agent for it, and you have the numbers to decide what's next.

items.title: Map and wrap
items.label: Week 1
items.text: Capability map, first ten tools against staging, guardrail design.

items.title: Guard and embed
items.label: Week 2
items.text: Policy hooks, approvals, audit log; the chat inside your app behind your login.

items.title: Pilot
items.label: Week 3
items.text: Three to five people use it for real work. We review transcripts and costs, then fix what they hit.

items.question: Will it make things up?
items.answer: It looks things up through your tools instead of answering from memory, and it's told to say when a tool finds nothing. Numbers come from your systems and are shown to people as the tool returned them, in tables and charts the model doesn't retype.

items.question: What if it does something wrong?
items.answer: Read-only tools run freely. Anything that changes data stops for a person's approval, with the exact details shown. Hooks block what policy forbids, whatever the model asks for, and the audit log records every action with the approver.

items.question: Do we have to throw away our admin panel?
items.answer: No. Most teams start with the floating widget next to the existing panel, then move workflows across as people stop opening the old screens.

items.question: Can our data stay on our own servers?
items.answer: Yes. The agent server runs in your infrastructure, and it can use local models (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM) or your cloud account's Azure OpenAI or Bedrock, so prompts and data never reach a third party you haven't chosen.

items.question: What does it cost to run?
items.answer: A typical admin task costs a fraction of a cent to a few cents in model tokens, and every run reports its own usage. Local models cost only the hardware.

items.question: Which stacks do you support?
items.answer: The chat comes as components for Vue 3, React (18 and 19) and Angular (21 and 22), and as a ready-made plugin for Strapi 5. The agent server is Node (TypeScript) on the MIT-licensed pi agent harness. The protocol is plain HTTP and server-sent events, so a .NET back end is a straightforward addition.

The agent server runs the pi agent loop with hooks, approvals, subagents, schedules and sessions, and calls your systems as tools, MCP servers, and model providers.
